studies.task: Write four short English texts of at least 50 words each: favorite food, favorite public figure, favorite festival or holiday, and an email requesting leave from a boss.

estimates.outcome: Cross-culture cosine similarity between Indian and American essays
estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of 3072-dimensional OpenAI text embeddings; the embedding model name is not specified. Each distribution includes every Indian-American essay pair on the same topic within an AI condition, pooled across topics. Higher values mean more similar writing across people.
estimates.treatment_arm: Indians with AI x Americans with AI (cross-culture pairs, both writers had AI)
estimates.control_arm: Indians without AI x Americans without AI (cross-culture pairs, neither writer had AI)

paper_effect.standardizer: Not stated. The reported analysis compares distributions of essay-pair similarities; no participant-level standardizer is reported.

estimates.notes: This is the main cross-culture similarity comparison, using both recruited cohorts. SDs are across essay pairs, not participants. The t-test treats pair scores as observations; participants contribute multiple essays and recur in many pairs, and no participant clustering is reported. The negative t statistic and Cohen’s d are transcribed as printed and correspond to the paper’s No AI versus AI ordering; they have not been re-signed. The paper prints 2784 control-condition pairs but does not print the AI or combined pair count, so n_units is null. Figure 6(b) shows 95% intervals, but their endpoints are not printed and are not read from the graph. The combined control participant count is not printed and has not been calculated from the country cells. The raw mean difference and its uncertainty are not printed.

estimates.outcome: Classifier accuracy distinguishing Indian from American authorship, all tasks (%)
estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: A logistic-regression classifier predicts Indian versus American authorship from 3072-dimensional OpenAI essay embeddings, fitted separately to AI and No AI essays. Stratified cross-validation produces 20 scores per condition. Scores are recorded as printed percentages, not proportions. Each observation for the comparison is a fold-level score on a set of essays; higher performance indicates greater cultural distinguishability across people.
estimates.treatment_arm: AI condition (Indians with AI and Americans with AI), all four tasks
estimates.control_arm: No AI condition (Indians without AI and Americans without AI), all four tasks

stats.difference_is: Decrease from No AI to AI, in percentage points: control minus treatment, as printed.

paper_effect.standardizer: Not stated. Cohen’s d compares distributions of cross-validation accuracy scores, not participant-level outcomes.

open_items: Counts at random assignment and post-assignment attrition are not reported. Inclusion required completing the writing tasks and demographic survey and being born in and a lifelong resident of the recruited country (PDF pp. 4-5, Sections 3.3 and 3.4).
The combined No AI participant count is not printed, although Table 1 prints the country-specific control counts. It is left null rather than added or subtracted from other counts.

Participant-level SDs, SEs and participant-clustered uncertainty are absent. Similarity uncertainty is based on essay pairs and classifier uncertainty on model-performance scores; these records do not provide participant-level precision for pooling.

For cross-culture similarity the AI and combined pair counts are not printed, and the plotted mean-confidence-interval endpoints are not numerically labeled. No counts are inferred from degrees of freedom and no graph values are digitized.

Classifier arm SDs and SEs and effect-size SEs/intervals are not printed. A per-condition fold count is printed for the all-task analysis, but no combined count; the email-specific fold count is not stated.
The paper does not state the standardizer used for its Cohen’s d values. Printed signs follow No AI versus AI ordering and are retained unchanged.
GPT-4o is named, but its release year and dated API snapshot are not stated; ai_tool.year is null. The OpenAI embedding model is not named.

The public-figure aggregate in the prose conflicts with the displayed AI-column counts in Appendix B, Table 7. That Indian-only outcome is excluded as a subgroup result; the discrepancy remains unresolved.
The citation record identifies a later ACM version of record. Differences from the saved arXiv v3 have not been verified.

Country-only effects, including within-culture similarity and one-cohort direction-of-homogenization contrasts, are treated as subgroup results under the extraction brief. The screening form lists them as contrasts, but country is a recruited cohort rather than a randomized AI configuration.
notes: Extraction date: 2026-10-09. Read the entire markdown conversion, including references and appendices, and checked all recorded numerical results on the cited PDF pages using pymupdf. One randomized experiment is analyzed; the paper’s later similarity and predictive-modeling experiments reuse its participants. The screening form’s country-by-condition cell names are retained, while the recorded estimates use both country cohorts. Participants were randomly assigned at consent to AI or No AI (PDF p. 4, Section 3.3.1); country was not assigned. Only full-sample numeric output contrasts are recorded; email-only measures use a task completed by the whole sample and are not participant-subgroup analyses. The saved article reports no preregistration, shared participant sample, or data/code repository. The writing task is included through the cross-person similarity criterion; no rated creativity or after-AI outcome is reported. All values retain the paper’s printed units and signs; no effects, uncertainties, aggregate counts or missing standard deviations have been calculated.
